title: How to handle Privacy Policy as a solo AI game developer?
author: Old_Peak_1332
selftext: I'm working on an educational game and am doing it basically all using Claude. It excells at a lot of things, but one thing I'm scared of is all the legal documents you have to have. My game is nothing special and doesnt handle any sensitive data, but I have no experience in this and I don't trust AI to do it for me. Claude says to consult legal experts, but that seems very expensive as someone with no budget. How have you handeled it if you've been in the same situation?

comments.author: Outside_The_Playtrix
comments.body: I don’t think it’s that complicated. I would just do some deep research and use it to make a plan and then have the plan checked and then carry out the plan. You aren’t handling sensitive data after all so it doesn’t apply to you in spirit, you just have to triple check you’ve ticked all the boxes. I think OpenAI is releasing a specialist law AI soon too apparently

comments.author: InsolentCoolRadio
comments.body:
\#0 I am NOT a lawyer and this is NOT legal advice 

\#1 Everything is expensive if you don’t research how much it costs. Almost everything is cheaper than infinity, which is the current quote you’re giving yourself

\#2 Research the risks involved, decide your own risk tolerance, and how much money you’re willing to spend on legal help, books on the subject, or another AI to check your first AI’s legal work

\#3 Make a plan based on those things.

\#4 Offset costs by researching free legal helps, borrowing the books you need from the library, and using freemium versions of frontier LLMs

\#5 Execute.

\#6 See #0.

comments.author: Mindestiny
comments.body:
Simple - collect no personal information at all and you have no obligation.

Whatever platform you're distributing on is the one that has the obligation when it comes to payment info, privacy records, etc.

Without knowing anything about your game, unless you have some sort of multiplayer component or you're doing micro transactions or otherwise collecting personal data on users, there's nothing to comply with.  Don't collect it and there's no oblgiation

replies.author: gefahr
replies.body: You still need a privacy policy.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
For what? You're literally not collecting user data.  Zero data.

The *sales and distribution* platform needs one.  But that's not the developers responsibility.

replies.author: Key_Confusion_576
replies.body:
while this may be technically correct, the policy at the distributor might require one anyway.   
its pretty common, especially in mobile.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body: "This app does not collect any personally identifiable user data or any app usage data via installation or usage."  That's it.  That's the whole policy if Google Play makes you state it. No legal quagmire, no expensive lawyers.

replies.author: Key_Confusion_576
replies.body:
What exactly are you even saying to me?
I don't speak meds. Sorry.

Bottom line is, you need one. Personally, I wouldn't trust your arm chair diagnosis of the situation. I hope OP listens to someone with real experience telling them to use one of the available templates or see what similar apps do.
Why wouldn't you just take some time to make sure things are propper?

comments.author: gefahr
comments.body: There are free, reusable templates online. Pick one and make sure it matches any data collection you're doing. Done.

comments.author: shuozhe
comments.body:
Do not trust a single model or a session with existing context. Check for every region/country you want to release.

And check what other games did, especially the one with a somewhat know publisher

comments.author: SalvorAdrift
comments.body: not a lawyer, but the cheapest fix is to collect nothing at all, then your policy is one short page saying so, and the storefront handles payment data on their end. the one place i would be careful is that an educational game can pull in kids, and rules for anything aimed at under 13 are a lot stricter, so that is the part worth paying someone to look at rather than the rest. if you do end up collecting anything, write down exactly what and why first, because that list is most of the policy anyway.

comments.author: iubenda_team
comments.body:
To settle the split on whether you even need one: you probably do, even collecting nothing yourself. The app stores require a privacy policy to publish, and most analytics/ad SDKs you'd add collect data on their end, so "I collect nothing" usually stops being true once you ship.

The part genuinely worth care, and someone already nailed it: an educational game likely reaches under-13s, and kids' privacy rules are much stricter (COPPA in the US, GDPR's rules for minors in the EU), parental consent, no behavioral ads to children. That's where the real exposure is, and worth a little budget.

For the standard case on no budget: a free policy generator produces one matching what you and your SDKs actually collect, no lawyer needed. (We make one, disclosure: we're iubenda, but any reputable one works.) Save the budget for the kids angle.
